power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Perceived treatability is not evidence of diagnostic validity and benefit: A response to Hastings and Hahn on borderline personality disorder

author.affiliation:
Independent Researcher Sydney
								
									New South Wales
									Australia

text.text: Hastings and Hahn report that a borderline personality disorder (BPD) label can improve selected treatment beliefs among clinical psychology trainees.
However, more favourable clinician expectations should not be interpreted as evidence that receiving the diagnosis benefits patients.
Perceived treatability, treatment efficacy, treatment safety, and patient benefit are distinct constructs.

This distinction is particularly important given documented negative effects associated with dialectical behaviour therapy and broader limitations in the systematic assessment and reporting of treatment-related harm in psychotherapy research.

Hastings and Hahn's vignette design also presupposes rather than evaluates the legitimacy of the BPD construct and cannot address diagnostic bias, harms arising from classification, or the lived consequences of diagnosis and subsequent care.
Their findings therefore demonstrate a change in selected clinician beliefs, not improved care or net patient benefit.
Claims of diagnostic benefit require evidence addressing treatment safety, patient-defined outcomes, diagnostic validity and bias, and lived experience.
-More favourable clinician beliefs about treatability should not be interpreted as evidence that a BPD diagnosis benefits patients.
-Evidence of psychotherapy efficacy should be considered alongside treatment safety, including documented negative effects of DBT and limitations in harm monitoring.
-Clinical implications of BPD diagnosis require attention to diagnostic bias, treatment-related harm, informed consent, and lived consequences of diagnosis and care.
Perceived treatability is not patient benefit Hastings and Hahn (2026) provide useful evidence that a BPD label can improve selected treatment beliefs among clinical psychology trainees.
text.formatted: Perceived treatability is not patient benefit <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Hastings and Hahn (2026)</ref> provide useful evidence that a BPD label can improve selected treatment beliefs among clinical psychology trainees.

text.text: In their vignette experiment, diagnosis increased perceived treatability and, for younger patients, improved expectations about the therapeutic relationship, while most measured cognitive, emotional, and distancing responses were unaffected.

However, the suggestion that people receiving a BPD diagnosis may benefit from more positive treatment expectations moves from a measured outcome, clinician belief, toward an unmeasured one, patient benefit.
Their design establishes that a label can alter selected trainee expectations.
It cannot establish that receiving the diagnosis improves care, outcomes, or safety.
This distinction matters because Hastings and Hahn (2026) suggest that the availability of effective evidence-based treatments may partly explain more favourable beliefs about diagnosed patients.
text.formatted: This distinction matters because <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Hastings and Hahn (2026)</ref> suggest that the availability of effective evidence-based treatments may partly explain more favourable beliefs about diagnosed patients.

text.text: Perceived treatability, treatment efficacy, and treatment safety are distinct constructs.

Psychological therapy research has historically prioritised benefit over systematic assessment of treatment-related harm, producing an asymmetrical evidence base in which safety cannot be inferred from efficacy alone (Cobbaert, 2026).
text.formatted: Psychological therapy research has historically prioritised benefit over systematic assessment of treatment-related harm, producing an asymmetrical evidence base in which safety cannot be inferred from efficacy alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Cobbaert, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In 132 randomised controlled trials, 79% gave no indication that treatment-related harm was monitored (Jonsson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In 132 randomised controlled trials, 79% gave no indication that treatment-related harm was monitored <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Jonsson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A later systematic review identified 1,430 relevant publications, but only 57 extracted original studies had monitored potential negative effects (Honkalampi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A later systematic review identified 1,430 relevant publications, but only 57 extracted original studies had monitored potential negative effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Honkalampi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The issue is directly relevant to DBT, a treatment predominantly associated with BPD. Lawson and Farquharson (2025) found that clients and staff described negative effects including pathologisation and retraumatisation, with participants reporting that DBT made them feel disempowered and silenced, emphasizing the need for recognition of potential harms and meaningful informed consent.
text.formatted: The issue is directly relevant to DBT, a treatment predominantly associated with BPD. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Lawson and Farquharson (2025)</ref> found that clients and staff described negative effects including pathologisation and retraumatisation, with participants reporting that DBT made them feel disempowered and silenced, emphasizing the need for recognition of potential harms and meaningful informed consent.

text.text: Their qualitative study cannot estimate prevalence or establish that DBT is harmful for all people.
It does establish that treatment-related harm is a clinically relevant outcome that efficacy data alone cannot resolve.
A diagnosis that increases clinicians' willingness or confidence to treat may increase treatment exposure, but treatment exposure is not itself evidence of benefit.
Hastings and Hahn's design also presupposes rather than tests diagnostic legitimacy.
Their vignette was constructed as a presentation already considered consistent with BPD, after which the diagnostic label was manipulated.

This appropriately isolates a labelling effect, but cannot determine whether the experiences should have been conceptualised as BPD in the first place, whether bias affects who receives the label, or whether classification itself produces harm.
These questions are not peripheral.

A critical discourse analysis argues that BPD diagnostic discourse can obscure trauma, sensory differences, and structural determinants of distress while reproducing gendered, cisheteronormative, and neuronormative assumptions (Cobbaert et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A critical discourse analysis argues that BPD diagnostic discourse can obscure trauma, sensory differences, and structural determinants of distress while reproducing gendered, cisheteronormative, and neuronormative assumptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cobbaert et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Critical scholarship on transgender healthcare similarly warns that value-laden personality disorder constructs can pathologise responses to discrimination and gender-related distress and may obstruct access to gender-affirming care (Porter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Critical scholarship on transgender healthcare similarly warns that value-laden personality disorder constructs can pathologise responses to discrimination and gender-related distress and may obstruct access to gender-affirming care <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Porter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical evidence also indicates diagnostic disparity: lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients were more likely than heterosexual patients to receive a BPD diagnosis even after adjustment for relevant clinical correlates (Rodriguez-Seijas et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence also indicates diagnostic disparity: lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients were more likely than heterosexual patients to receive a BPD diagnosis even after adjustment for relevant clinical correlates <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Rodriguez-Seijas et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Lived experience evidence further shows why clinician optimism cannot stand in for patient benefit. Aves (2024) describes, as an autistic woman, actively monitoring language and behaviour to avoid being mislabelled with BPD, alongside long-term iatrogenic harm, loss of trust, and eventual service avoidance.
text.formatted: Lived experience evidence further shows why clinician optimism cannot stand in for patient benefit. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Aves (2024)</ref> describes, as an autistic woman, actively monitoring language and behaviour to avoid being mislabelled with BPD, alongside long-term iatrogenic harm, loss of trust, and eventual service avoidance.

text.text: Warrender (2025) similarly documents diagnostic confusion, self-stigma, diagnostic overshadowing, and exclusion from therapy among people diagnosed with BPD.
Such consequences can coexist with more favourable clinician beliefs about treatability.
Hastings and Hahn's findings challenge the assumption that a BPD label inevitably worsens treatment attitudes among contemporary clinical psychology trainees.
They do not establish that receiving the diagnosis improves care or produces net patient benefit.

That conclusion would require evidence concerning patient-defined outcomes, actual treatment access and outcomes, treatment-related harm, informed consent, diagnostic validity and bias, and the lived consequences of classification and care.
More favourable professional expectations should therefore be interpreted as a change in clinician beliefs, not as a proxy for diagnostic benefit.
No funding was obtained for this work.
No data was used for the research described in the article.
Laurence Cobbaert: Conceptualisation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Project administration, Writing -original draft, Writing -review and editing
This work does not involve the collection of human data.
